Tchaikovsky: Guide to the Practical Study of Harmony

The modulation examples, with Roman numerals under the notes

The 25 modulation examples from Tchaikovsky’s Guide to the Practical Study of Harmony (1872), short four-voice progressions from C major to keys near and far, with the Roman-numeral analysis under the notes (When in Rome). Play each one.

Tchaikovsky wrote his harmony textbook in 1871 from his lectures at the Moscow Conservatory; Jurgenson published it in 1872, and in English in 1900. These are its modulation examples: each starts in C major and reaches another key, near or far, in a few chords. They are grouped by the book’s example number.

How to read the labels and use the scores: Analysed Scores. For modulation itself, see Chapter 22.

173i. C major to A major

NoteFor teachers
  • Source: the notes and analyses are the DDMAL Key Modulation Dataset’s encodings of the book’s examples (Néstor Nápoles López and others), translated automatically to RomanText and copied into When in Rome. scripts/when-in-rome/build.mjs reads the MusicXML (src/tchaikovsky), and every note was checked against music21’s reading of the same files.
  • Example 185a uses im7, a minor seventh chord on the tonic of the new key; it is shown as written.
  • Not edited: the analyses are an automated translation and are shown as they are.

For students

Gotham, Mark, et al. When in Rome: A Meta-Corpus of Functional Harmony. GitHub. github.com/MarkGotham/When-in-Rome. The analyses on this page (RomanText files), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Hutchinson, Robert. “Modulation.” Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom, ch. 22, U of Puget Sound. musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Modulation.html. Tonicization against modulation, closely related keys, diatonic and chromatic pivot chords, and direct, common-tone and sequential modulation.

Tchaikovsky Research. “Guide to the Practical Study of Harmony.” en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Guide_to_the_Practical_Study_of_Harmony. When and how Tchaikovsky wrote the book (1871, from his Moscow Conservatory lectures); Jurgenson, 1872; English translation by Emil Krall and James Liebling, 1900.

For teachers

Nápoles López, Néstor, et al. Key Modulation Dataset. GitHub (DDMAL). github.com/DDMAL/key_modulation_dataset. The encodings and analyses of the textbook examples, translated to RomanText by Nápoles López and copied into When in Rome.
